posts.title: What happens at the Saturday swatch table
posts.excerpt: Hands-on testing, comparing undertones, and seeing how wet emulsion shifts as it dries.
posts.content:
Every Saturday between 10:00 and 13:00 Mei sets up a long table by the window with sample boards, brushes and a pot of every finish we mix. Visitors paint a board, set it against the wall photo on their phone and watch it dry.

Wet paint always reads darker and cooler than dry paint. The table is there so that you see the change before you buy a tin. Pieter de Wit runs a short brushwork demonstration on the first Saturday of the month.

posts.title: Why we sell a sample pot before a tin
posts.excerpt: Testing 100 ml on your own wall prevents costly mistakes under real room light.
posts.content:
A sample pot is 100 ml of any colour, mixed to order, for €6. It is enough for a card or a square metre of wall.

Lena writes the recipe for the pot and keeps it on file, so if the colour works the tin is mixed from the same recipe. If it does not, the sample cost you less than a tin of the wrong green.

posts.title: One green, two rooms: north light and south light
posts.excerpt: How exposure and shadow change the perception of a single moss recipe.
posts.content:
The same recipe went onto a north-facing kitchen in Kralingen and a south-facing living room in Noord. In the kitchen it read grey and cool; in the living room it read warm and almost yellow.

Amara matched the kitchen one step warmer after the drawdown check. The lesson is the one the shop is built on: a colour is chosen against the room, not the chip.

posts.title: Hanging the first drop straight
posts.excerpt: Why the first strip decides the whole wall.
posts.content:
Tomás starts every wall with a plumb line, not the corner. Corners are rarely straight, and a paper hung from the corner drifts.

Paste the wall, hang the first drop to the line, smooth from the centre out with a wide brush and check the seam against the second drop before the paste sets. Order every roll from one batch, plus one spare.

posts.title: Drawdown cards, and why we wait twenty minutes
posts.excerpt: At our Verfstraat counter, we paint a drawdown card for every mixed sample and wait twenty minutes for the wet sheen to clear before checking the shade by the window.
posts.content:
When a customer steps up to the mixing counter at Verfstraat 18 with a paint flake, a torn piece of linen, or a photo on their phone, the instinct is often to rush. People want to see the colourant drop from the tinting machine nozzle, watch the canister shake, and leave immediately with a fresh tin under their arm. But at Toso Paints, we never hand across a freshly mixed colour without painting a drawdown card first. And once that card is painted, we place it on a drying rack by the window and wait twenty minutes.

The reason is grounded in the basic physics of paint emulsion. Wet paint reflects surface glare. The water content creates an artificial sheen that scatters overhead shop light, making any wet pigment appear lighter and more milky than it will look once cured on a wall. If Lena Brandt were to read the wet formula and declare the match complete, the resulting room would almost certainly turn out darker, heavier, or colder than expected. House Matt, our washable flat emulsion, undergoes a marked shift as its water evaporates, settling into its true velvety depth. Our Wood & Metal Eggshell and mineral Lime Wash behave similarly, revealing their genuine undertones only after the liquid vehicle has cleared.

Those twenty minutes of waiting are where the actual craft happens. Lena draws a measured layer of paint across a rigid test card using a steel drawdown bar, producing a clean, uniform film of consistent thickness. The card goes onto a slim rack positioned beside our tall, north-facing workshop window. We never evaluate colour under fluorescent tubes or warm shop spotlights. Retail bulbs distort chromatic balance, hiding green undertones beneath amber warmth or deadening subtle greys. Daylight from a Dutch sky is honest, diffuse, and steady.

We saw this principle clearly in a recent consultation for a north kitchen in Kralingen. The homeowner arrived with a phone photo showing an old olive green wall. After Lena formulated the initial recipe and mixed a 100 ml sample pot, the wet paint looked convincingly close on the stirring stick. But when the drawdown card dried twenty minutes later beside the window, the cool northern daylight revealed that the green had leaned too sharp and acidic for a Rotterdam kitchen. Standing together at the counter, Ines Valk and the customer agreed to adjust the recipe one step warmer. Lena altered the tinting formula, logged the adjustment in our permanent archive, and mixed the revised 2.5 L tin of House Matt. The finished room in Kralingen captured the calm warmth the owners wanted because the colour was judged dry, against natural light.

On Saturdays, this same patient testing extends to our swatch table between 10:00 and 13:00. Mei Lindgren sets out sample boards, brushes, and pots for visitors who want to compare shades side by side before ordering. Decorators and neighbours sit together, applying coats of Lime Wash or Wood & Metal Eggshell, watching the pigments dry under changing Rotterdam cloud cover. There is no guesswork involved, and no hurried decisions made under artificial lamps. Every recipe number is recorded on the lid and filed away, so when an extra tin is needed later, the exact tone can be reproduced without variation.

This methodical step forms the core of our shop philosophy: a colour is chosen against the room, not the chip. Whether you bring in a sample of wallpaper, an architectural tile, or a flake of plaster, twenty minutes by the window ensures that what leaves our counter in a tin matches the reality of your living space.

posts.title: Eggshell on old skirting
posts.excerpt: Preparing old woodwork for a low-sheen finish.
posts.content:
Wood & Metal Eggshell is a low-sheen finish for skirting, doors and radiators, sold in 1 L for €34. On old gloss, sand lightly, wipe, and prime any bare patches.

Two thin coats beat one thick coat. Leave it overnight before it meets a vacuum cleaner.

products.name: House Matt
products.short: A deep-matt wall paint, mixed to your colour at the counter, 2.5 L.
products.description:
House Matt is our washable, flat matt emulsion formulated specifically for interior walls and ceilings. Mixed to order in any shade at our Verfstraat counter.

What are the finish specifications and coverage for House Matt?

House Matt dries to an exceptionally flat, non-reflective finish that hides minor plaster imperfections while remaining durable and washable for daily living. Supplied in 2.5 L metal tins for €58, this water-based emulsion covers about 12 m² per litre per coat. It is formulated for interior walls and ceilings in busy family homes, dining areas, and living spaces. Mixed paint is ready to collect at our shop in 2 hours. Delivery throughout Rotterdam is €9, or free on orders over €150. Clean brushes thoroughly with clean water immediately after application.

How should House Matt be sampled and ordered?

We always recommend sampling your colour before buying full tins. A 100 ml Sample Pot can be mixed in any bespoke recipe for €6. Paint a test board, let it dry thoroughly, and observe how the pigment responds to changing morning and evening light in your room. Orders placed before 15:00 Tuesday to Saturday are dispatched for next working day delivery in Rotterdam. Lena Brandt writes the unique recipe number onto the lid of every mixed tin and logs it in our workshop file, making exact re-ordering effortless whenever you decide to decorate adjacent rooms.
